**`&&` is what makes that nested case a conflict.** Both comparisons have to be true at the same time.

Take 13:00–14:00 vs 13:20–13:40:

- `13:20 < 14:00` — the inner slot starts before the outer one ends
- `13:40 > 13:00` — the inner slot ends after the outer one starts

Both are true, so it is a conflict. The same two checks also cover partial overlap (13:00–14:00 vs 13:30–15:00).

`||` would be wrong. A 13:00–14:00 slot and a 15:00–16:00 slot do not overlap, but `16:00 > 13:00` is still true, so `||` would flag them as a conflict.

Two ranges overlap only when each one starts before the other ends. Touching times (14:00–15:00 next to 13:00–14:00) fail one of the two checks, which is why they are not conflicts.

</user_query>

This loop copies the current slot onto every resource that its resource **blocks**. It runs once per slot, after that slot has already been added to its own resource.

**`for (const dep of dependencies)`** — walk every row in `BlockingDependencies` (`blocking_resource_id` → `blocked_resource_id`).

**`if (dep.blockingResourceId !== slot.resourceId) continue;`** — skip rows that are not about this slot. Example: a Pool slot only cares about rows where Pool is the blocker (Pool → Lane 1, Pool → Lane 2, …). A Lane 1 row is ignored for a Pool slot.

**`let blocked = result.find(...)`** — look up the resource this row blocks in the grouped result (Lane 1 if Pool blocks Lane 1).

**`if (!blocked) { blocked = { resourceId, slots: [] }; result.push(blocked); }`** — if that resource has no entry yet (Lane 4 has no bookings of its own), create an empty group so there is somewhere to put the copy.

**`blocked.slots.push({ ...slot, conflicts: [] });`** — copy this slot onto the blocked resource. `{ ...slot }` is a new object so Pool’s own list and Lane 1’s list do not share the same object. `conflicts` stays empty here; the next loop fills it after all copies exist.

Net effect: a Pool booking shows up on Pool **and** on every lane Pool blocks. Blocking is one-way, so Lane 1 bookings are not copied onto Pool.

<timestamp>Thursday, Aug 20, 2026, 2:52 PM (UTC+3)</timestamp>
<user_query>
explainthe changes
</user_query>

Copies of one booking used to get **different** `conflicts` arrays. Now every copy of the same slot id gets the **same** list.

**What was wrong**

Conflicts were computed only inside each resource’s list. A Pool booking copied to Lane 1, Lane 2, and Pool was treated as three separate slots:

- On Lane 1 it picked up overlapping Lane 1 bookings
- On Pool it only saw other Pool bookings
- On Lane 2 it only saw Lane 2 bookings

So one copy could look conflicted and another copy of the same slot could look free.

**What it does now**

1. Same as before: find time overlaps **per resource** (who sits next to whom on that calendar).
2. **Merge by slot id.** If the Pool booking clashes on Lane 1, that clash is stored under that slot’s id. If it also clashes on Lane 2, that clash is added to the same list (duplicates skipped).
3. Write that one list onto **every copy** of that id.

The `{ ...other, conflicts: [] }` copies are only so JSON does not cycle (`A.conflicts → B.conflicts → A`).

**Example**

Pool “Aqua Aerobics” 09:30–11:00 overlaps Lane 1 “Private Coaching”. After the merge, the Pool copy on Pool, Lane 1, Lane 2, Lane 3, and Lane 4 all list Private Coaching. Same slot, same conflicts, everywhere it appears.

Yes. Same behavior, three steps:

1. **Group** — Map of resource → slots. Each slot goes on its own resource and on every resource it blocks.
2. **Link pairs once** — For two slots in the same group, if the other starts later and still starts before this one ends, record both ids in a `Set` (no `filter`/`some`, no duplicate objects).
3. **Attach** — Every copy of a slot id gets that same id list, turned into plain slot objects so JSON does not cycle.

The old version did find-or-create twice, stored full slot objects while merging, and scanned arrays to skip duplicates. Sets and a Map replace all of that.

@server/src/slots/slots.service.ts:52-59 explain both

These two blocks record the **same clash in both directions**. We only detect the pair once (the later-starting slot), so we have to write both sides by hand.

**First block — `slot` → `other`**

```
fromSlot = conflictIds for this slot (or a new Set)
fromSlot.add(other.id)
save it
```

“This slot conflicts with `other`.” Example: Pool Aqua Aerobics lists Lane 1 Private Coaching.

**Second block — `other` → `slot`**

Same thing flipped: `other`’s set gets `slot.id`.

“`other` conflicts with this slot.” Private Coaching lists Aqua Aerobics.

Without the second block, only the earlier slot would show a conflict. `Set` means adding the same id twice (because the slot is copied onto several resources) does not create duplicates.

<timestamp>Thursday, Aug 20, 2026, 3:04 PM (UTC+3)</timestamp>
<user_query>
@server/src/slots/slots.service.ts:66-75 and this
</user_query>

This builds the API response: one entry per resource, each slot with its `conflicts` filled in.

**`[...groups.entries()].map(([resourceId, group]) => ({ ... }))`**  
`groups` is `resourceId → slots`. Spread turns the Map into `[resourceId, group]` pairs, then each pair becomes `{ resourceId, slots }`.

**`slots: group.map((slot) => ({ ...slot, conflicts: ... }))`**  
Keep the slot as-is (including copies on blocked resources) and replace `conflicts`.

**`[...(conflictIds.get(slot.id) ?? [])]`**  
Look up that slot’s conflict **ids**. `?? []` means none. Spread turns the `Set` into an array. Every copy of the same id gets this same list.

**`.map((id) => slotById.get(id))`**  
Turn each id into the original slot from the database.

**`.filter((other): other is Slot => other !== undefined)`**  
Drop ids that were not found (TypeScript also narrows the type).

**`.map((other) => ({ ...other, conflicts: [] }))`**  
Return a **new** object with empty `conflicts` so JSON does not cycle (`A.conflicts → B.conflicts → A`).

Example: Aqua Aerobics is copied onto Pool and Lane 1. Both copies use `conflictIds.get(aquaId)`, so both list Private Coaching.
